research_concepts: opponent next-possession PPP after a play type (downstream suppression/aftershock)
possession ending state and boundary drift
play-type labeling artifacts (foul endings, OTHER bucket)
methodological_questions: Is the opponent next-possession PPP shift attributable to play type X, large enough to change an AVOID label once direct PPP is counted?
Do own-sequence lags survive team-season demeaning and decay checks?
How can the effect be separated from ending state (make/miss/live turnover), foul and free-throw endings, game state and team quality?
What sample size and multiplicity control are needed per play type and lag?

historical_evidence.finding: Extended Possession Value: opponent T+1 suppression was 'real' for 4 of 8 play types (CUT +0.0220, TRANSITION +0.0145, SPOT_UP +0.0124, POST_UP +0.0194). DRIVE was not real (opp ATT +0.0024). The record notes downstream effects are small (~0.01-0.02 PPP) relative to direct PPP gaps, and player-level effects are mostly non-findings after BH.

Descriptive. Ending state changes opponent output in the next 90s; live turnovers shift opponent possession count (dOppPoss +0.298) much more than PPP (dOppPPP +0.055). Boundary drift is described as ~0.01-0.02 PPP. No inferential tests.
Own-team lag curves: global lifts (e.g. SPOT_UP lag-1 +0.027) were flat and non-decaying and disappeared after team-season demeaning. Within-team memory was essentially none except SPOT_UP lag-1.

The Level 1 gate for decaying cross-possession memory failed. DRIVE lifts were flat (+0.015 to +0.021), Cohen d ~0.01-0.03, and callable play-type horizons = 0. The effect collapsed under a within-team baseline (team-quality confound).

After the opponent runs X, the next offensive play type Y scores above its baseline. 'Defensive aftershock' was reported for 8/8 play types at about +0.12 to +0.13 in all games and playoffs, with limited sample in some pair cells. These values are close to uniform across play types.

Labeling audit: OTHER has 36% foul endings (PPP inflated); DRIVE sits 12pp below the foul benchmark (foul leakage); PNR has a 22% foul rate. Only 0.7% of 50,668 possessions map to a real play type via initiation_type.
Lag-1 ATT of +0.204 after a star's 2nd foul was a free-throw composition artifact (FT share 41.8% vs 9.9%). Without FTs the effect was +0.049 and not significant.
Star-level suppression after opponent play types (e.g. PUTBACK) rests on cells with n_after of 32-95 and no multiplicity correction.
Rank-1 suppressor deltas were mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; an OTHER artifact was flagged.
A single-pair spillover test (Brown to Tatum) was null/inconclusive: ATT inside the placebo range, signs flipping across splits.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Global (non-demeaned) lag-curve lifts used as evidence of own-sequence memory
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact: flat, non-decaying lifts vanish after team-season demeaning.
Flat lifts with tiny effect sizes, significant only because n>150k; team-quality confound.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using raw play-type PPP including foul-ending possessions and the OTHER bucket
failed_approaches.why: Foul endings inflate or deflate PPP, which is a labeling/construction artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Lag effect estimated with free throws included
failed_approaches.why: Free-throw composition difference produced the entire apparent effect.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Per-star suppressor rankings from small cells
failed_approaches.why: No multiplicity correction and n_after of 32-95.

evidence_establishes: Per FAM:SF-APPS-075, downstream opponent-next-possession effects for play types are small (~0.01-0.02 PPP) and mixed across play types (DRIVE null) relative to direct PPP gaps.
Per FAM:SF-APPS-073 and FAM:SF-CHT-029, global own-sequence lag effects are artifacts of team quality; within-team memory is essentially absent (SPOT_UP lag-1 the possible exception).
Per FAM:SF-APPS-078, much of the post-possession opponent cost comes through possession volume and ending state, not PPP.
Per FAM:SF-CHT-025 and FAM:SF15, foul/FT composition and the OTHER bucket are known sources of artifacts in play-type PPP comparisons.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether any downstream effect flips a specific AVOID label. No retrieved record ran that decision-level comparison.
Whether the 2025-26 data replicate the earlier-season findings (the retrieved records do not state the seasons used).
The causal source of the SF07 aftershock of ~+0.12-0.13 across all play types; the record does not state how it was baselined.
Which of the 075 downstream effects remain after controlling for ending state and team quality; the record gives no validation status for that family.
own_inferences: The near-uniform +0.12-0.13 aftershock in SF07 across 8/8 play types suggests a shared baseline or ending-state component rather than play-type-specific signal. This is my inference, not stated in the record.
An effect of 0.01-0.02 PPP is probably too small to drive AVOID labels unless play types are separated by near-ties in direct PPP. This is my inference.
The 'large enough' claim is better treated as an equivalence/magnitude question than a null-hypothesis test, since with n>100k tiny effects will always be significant.

Opponent next-possession effects are mechanically tied to how the focal possession ended (made basket vs live turnover vs miss). Play types therefore differ in downstream PPP largely through ending-state mix, which is a mediator or confounder depending on the estimand.
uncertainties: No labeling-validity record for derived play types beyond the foul audit; initiation_type maps only 0.7% of possessions (per FAM:SF-CHT-025).
The AVOID label definition and threshold are not stated in the task, so 'large enough' is undefined.
The 2025-26 playoffs are partial on the question date (complete from 2026-06-21), so the final season is not usable as a clean holdout until then.
Historical records do not state the seasons used, so overlap with the current data is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I would have considered proceeding as posed. The records show downstream effects of ~0.01-0.02 PPP, own-lag effects that are team-quality artifacts, and known foul/FT labeling artifacts, so I moved to proceed_with_changes. The changes: reframe as a magnitude/label-flip question, use within-team baselines, stratify by ending state, and exclude FT/foul and OTHER possessions.

methodological_questions: Is opponent next-possession PPP after a play type large enough to drive AVOID labels?
Do own-sequence lags (previous possession play type) materially affect play-type efficiency?
How should next-possession and lag effects be separated from confounding by game state, team quality, and possession outcome (e.g., made basket vs miss, transition)?
What sample size and shrinkage are needed for play-type-level effects?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm settling on writing the final answer without more tool calls. The claim that the effects are large enough to drive AVOID labels doesn't hold up against the historical data: the downstream effects were only about 0.01 to 0.02 PPP, small next to the direct gaps, and the DRIVE effect isn't real. The own-sequence lag effects look like artifacts of team-quality confounding.

I'm checking the remaining results against the historical record: the SF07 aftershock looks like a uniform baseline rather than something that separates play types. The playoff data is incomplete as of the question date, so I'll hold out the 2025-26 regular season and test whether within-team suppression is large enough to flip an AVOID label.

I'm now laying out the design: possession-level comparisons that condition on how the possession ended, with team-season fixed effects and game-state controls, and excluding foul-ending and OTHER possessions. I'd set the decision rule as whether the downstream shift is large enough to move the PPP gap past the AVOID cutoff, with a pre-specified equivalence margin of about ±0.02 PPP. Sample sizes look adequate for the common play types, though PUTBACK would be noisier.

I'm setting up the lagged own-sequence comparisons within each team, correcting for multiple testing across the eight play types and their lags. I expect most of these to come back as rejected effects, though some may still look like artifacts.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm settling on writing the final answer without more tool calls. The claim that the effects are large enough to drive AVOID labels doesn't hold up against the historical data: the downstream effects were only about 0.01 to 0.02 PPP, small next to the direct gaps, and the DRIVE effect isn't real. The own-sequence lag effects look like artifacts of team-quality confounding.

I'm checking the remaining results against the historical record: the SF07 aftershock looks like a uniform baseline rather than something that separates play types. The playoff data is incomplete as of the question date, so I'll hold out the 2025-26 regular season and test whether within-team suppression is large enough to flip an AVOID label.

I'm now laying out the design: possession-level comparisons that condition on how the possession ended, with team-season fixed effects and game-state controls, and excluding foul-ending and OTHER possessions. I'd set the decision rule as whether the downstream shift is large enough to move the PPP gap past the AVOID cutoff, with a pre-specified equivalence margin of about ±0.02 PPP. Sample sizes look adequate for the common play types, though PUTBACK would be noisier.

I'm setting up the lagged own-sequence comparisons within each team, correcting for multiple testing across the eight play types and their lags. I expect most of these to come back as rejected effects, though some may still look like artifacts.
